  ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS  
Allegations on labour issues in BALCO  
*281 .   SHRI MOHAMMED AMIN:†† 
SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE: 
Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Ministry of Mines has forwarded allegat ions pertaining to labour related 
issues in the Bharat Aluminium Company Limited (BALCO) as stated in the report titled 
"Impact of Privatisation on Labour: A Study of BALCO Disinvestment" by V. V. Giri National 
Labuor Institute for inquiry; and 
if so, whether the inquiry has been completed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND  
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) and (b) A St atement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Study Report published by a researcher in V.V. Giri National Labour Institute 
does not mention any specific cases of violation of  labour laws; on this point no further 
action was, therefore, considered necessary. There have however been comments in the 
study about the payment of VRS and post VRS support. 
SHRI MOHAMMED AMIN: Sir, part (a) of my supplementary is, when is the summary of 
the report titled "Impact of Privatisation on Labou r: a Study of BALCO Disinvestment", 
published by V.V. Giri National Labour Institute sa ys, "Majority of the voluntary retired 
workers testify that they had to undergo several di rect and indirect pressurisatron tactics 
prior to their agreement to the voluntary separatio n scheme, during a phase of growing 
insecurities and ambiguities at the workplace.", th en how does the hon. Minister say that 
^he report is not specific about violation of labou r-related issues as per the Shareholders' 
\greement  between the Government and the Sterlite? 
Sir, part (b) of my supplementary is, whether the M inistry has seen the report of 
Council on Ethics, the Government Pension Fund—Glob al, Government of Norway, which 
specifically mentioned labour rights violation in BALCO by Sterlite Industries Limited, a 
subsidiary of Vedanta Resources, as reasons for dropping the said companies from sovereign 
wealth find? If so, why the Government is not takin g any action for cancellation of the 
Shareholders' Agreement with Sterlite.    
The question as actually asked on the floor of the House by SHRI Mohammed Amin.  

2    Oral  Answers  [RAJYA SABHA]  to Questions  
SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES: Sir, whatever VRS has been given, it has been given on the 
basis of applications submitted by the employees. There seems to be a lot of inconvenience 
caused to the imployees naturally; the Delhi office  employees were transferred to 
Chhattisgarh, and they were given a feeling that ev erything was not okay for them and 
they were asked for the VRS. But going by the figures of people who have accepted VRS, it 
looks, people who were very senior in service got t he VRS and not all the employees who 
asked for VRS got the VRS. Twenty-three employees who asked for VRS were not given the 
VRS.Aboutl302 people who asked for VRS were given t he VRS. Out of that, 1281 were ' 
given VRS in instalments which was not a correct th ing. But there was nothing in the 
Agreement that it should not be given. It is not a good practice to give VRS in instalments. 
They gave VRS in instalments of six months But, Sir , when the Study Report came, the « 
whole matter was over. The second stage of disinves tment is pending, and if there is 
anything to be done, it is for the Government to co nsider at this stage. But the first-stage 
agreement is over. It is implemented, and, 1 think, it is only for consideration at the second 
stage. 
  SHRI MOHAMMED AMIN: Sir, what we are experiencing in BALCO is a bitter result of 
privatisation. Here is a report which says, and, I quote, "Accusations against the company 
include labour rights violations, intimidation and harassment of workers, as well as forced 
eviction of tribal peoples from their villages. BAL CO is criticised for deplorable wage 
conditions and, in part, for dangerous working conditions at the Mainpat and Bodai-Daldali 
bauxite mines. Moreover, the company is accused of harassing striking workers and illegally 
cutting down 50,000 trees in connection with the expansion of the Korba project."

Criteria for conferring'Classical Language'status 
*282. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS bepleased 
to state: 
(a) the criterial for conferring 'Classical Language' status on a language; 
(b) the number of Indian languages conferred the status so far and the languages identified 
for the purpose; 
(c) whether there is demand for conferring the 'Classic al Language' status on Kannada 
and Tulu and inclusion of Tulu and Kodava languages  in the Eighth Schedule of the 
Constitution; and 
(d) if so, the details in this regard and Centre's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): (a) to (d) A Statement 
is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) The following criteria have been laid down for according classical status to a 
language:— 
(i)    High antiquity of its early texts/recorded history over a period of 1500—2000 
years. 
(ii)    A body of ancient literature/texts, which is considered a valuable heritage by 
generations of speakers. 
(iii)    The literary tradition be original and not borrowed from another speech community. 
(iv)    The classical language and literature being distinct from modem there may also be 
a discontinuity between the classical language and its later forms or its offshoots. 

Oral Answers  [5 DEC. 2007]  to Questions   5 
(b) So far the classical language status has been confe rred on two languages viz. Tamil 
and Sanskrit. No other language has been identified  for conferring the classical language 
status, so far. 
(c) and (d) The demand for conferring the 'Classical La nguage' status on Kannada has 
been referred by the Ministry of Culture to the 'Committee of Linguistic Experts' constituted 
in Sahitya Akademi for the purpose. No such demand has been received in respect of Tulu.

*283. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) the names of countries with which India has so far entered into Free Trade Agreement 
(FTAJ or similar agreements; and 
(b) the specific industries which have been adversely affected by these agreements? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE, MINISTRY OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) India has signed Free Trade Agreement (FTAs) with Sri Lanka, Singapore, Nepal and 
Bhutan. India has also signed South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) with Bangladesh, 

8    Oral  Answers  [RAJYA SABHA]  to Questions  
Bhutan, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. India has signed Preferential Trade Agreement 
(PTAs) with Afghanistan, Chile and MERCOSUR, and is  also signatory to the regional 
preferential trading agreement, namely, Asia Pacific Trade Agreement (Bangladesh, China, 
India, Republic of Korea, Lao PDR, Sri Lanka as members) & Global System of Trade Preference 
(open to all developing countries). India has an Early Harvest Scheme with Thailand where 
tariff concessions are exchanged on 82 products. 
(b) Some of the industries which complained being affected by the FTAs relate to Vanaspati, 
Copper, Zink Oxide from Nepal and Sri Lanka. Appropriate measures were put in place to 
safeguard their interests. 
SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Sir, there are some news paper reports that the 
Government intends to enter into an FTAor MFN kind of agreement with China, as part of its 
larger geo-political boundary dispute settlement with that country. I would like to know from 
the Minister whether this is true. If this is true,  would this not have a significant negative 
effect on the Indian small and medium scale industries? 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, the factual position is as follows. India has, as of now, five 
operational FTAs. It has six operational perferenti al trade agreements. Eleven FTAs are 
under negotiations and another seven are under consideration. The India-China FTA which 
the hon. Member is referred to falls under the category of FTAs being considered, not even 
being negotiated. I can assure the hon. Member that the decision to enter into an FTA with 
any country is taken after a great deal of consideration on which indusfries or which sectors 
of economy should be offered for liberalisation. 
SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the Minister then give us an assurance in this 
House that further FTAs will now only be entered into after carefiilly evaluating the effect of 
FTAs on the industries affected and prepare a roadmap of assistance for small and medium 
scale industries thus affected? 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, the hon. Member knows as an example that for the past 
three-and-a-half years, India has been negotiating an FTA with ASEAN. One of the reasons 
why we have not concluded the FTA has precisely been the need to protect sensitive sectors 
of our economy, particularly agriculture, textiles and small-scale industry. The assurance 
which the hon. Member seeks is implicit in the appr oach of the Government. The 
Government is extraordinarily careful in entering i nto these FTAs. I can assure the hon. 
Member that whatever FTA is entered into that is do ne in the most fransparent and most 
consultative manner. In fact, one of the criticisms against the FTA is that there is a very large 
negative list. The concept of negative list is that  we put into the negative list those items 
that are not subject to any form of liberalisation as part of free trade agreement. 
DR. E.M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN: Sir, Nepal has announced that they are ready 
to have an Indian rupee as part of the FTA transact ion. I would like to know whether the 
Government of India has got any proposal to have co mmon currency as part of FTA 
transaction, especially with SAFTA countries. 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, the question of common cur rency arises only after we 
progress beyond an FTA into a customs union and a common monetary union. As of now, 
our major task has been to stabilise and consolidate FTAs. We have had a trade treaty with 
Nepal for quite some time. It is working well. It has been entered into keeping in mind, not just 

Oral Answers  [5 DEC. 2007]  to Questions   9 
the economic relationship we have with Nepal, but more importantly the political and strategic 
importance of that country. 
SHRI PYARIMOHAN MOHAPATRA: Is the hon. Minister aware that by the Early Harvest 
Scheme, automobile component manufacturers and automobile mission, which the Prime 
Minister unveiled, are going to be affected severel y? Are there any complaints made by 
different associations of automobile component manufacturers? If so, what remedial steps are 
being initiated? 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, the Early Harvest Scheme, which the hon. Member is talking 
about, is a preferential trade agreement, which India has entered into with Thailand, where we are 
offering mutual tariff concessions on 82 items. I would just like to remind the hon. Member — I 
want to make here only a political point before I get into the economics of the trade agreement— 
that the Early Harvest Agreement was one of the agreements signed by the previous Government 
of which the BJD was a part. Since the Government is a continuing entity, we have continued with 
the Early Harvest Agreement. Now, Sir, under this agreement, 82 items have been given for 
liberalisation. In the last two-and-a-half years, it is true that imports from Thailand have gone up 
three-fold; whereas, exports from India have gone up only two-fold. So, prima facie, it might appear 
that this Early harvest Agreement has benefited Thailand more than it has benefited India. The 
numbers certainly bear it out. There are certain sectors of the economy like the auto components, 
electronic components, etc., where we have received complaints or Memoranda that this Early 
Harvest Agreement is working to our detriment. The reason for this is, we have an inverted duty 
structure. This is a legacy of the past. The legacy is that the duty on raw materials has been very 
high. The duty on components has been lower than that and the duty on fmished products has 
been the lowest. The Government of India has set up a Committee to look into all these imbalances 
in the duty structure. The duty structure and the anomalies are being rectified so that domestic 
manufacturing is not at a disadvantage, and it is not cheaper to import the fmished product, as 
supposed to be making those items at home. So, I would like to assure the hon. Member that the 
Early Harvest Agreement anomalies have been looked into most carefully. 
SHRI P.R. RAJAN: Sir, my supplementary is this. Would the hon. Minister be pleased to 
explain how these Free Trade Agreements affect the agricultural market in the country? The import 
of palm oil has already become a grave issue in Kerala. Again, what are the major provisions in 
the proposed trade agreement with the ASEAN? 
SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH: Sir, I would only be too pleased to answer this because this is a 
very sensitive issue as far as Kerala is concerned. I would like to assure all the hon. Members 
that on any Free' Trade Agreement, which has been n egotiated or is under negotiation, 
agriculture is in the negative list, this is a categorical statement that I am making, that all agricultural 
items, sensitive agricultural items particularly, are in the negative list. Now, as far as Kerala is 
concerned, there are sensitivities on spices, particularly; on rubber and a whole lot of plantation 
crops, these are not a part of the liberalisation programme. In fact, on the ASEAN Free Trade 
Agreement, India's offer is particularly on pepper. On cardamon, there is no liberalisation; on coconut, 
there is no liberalisation. In so far as pepper is concerned, the only offer that India has made to 
ASEAN is to reduce the existing level of import duty from 70 per cent to 50 per cent by the year 
2018, not today, but by the year 2018. So, I would like to assure the hon. Member that there is 
absolutely no question of liberalising the import o f agricultural commodities. The second 
supplementary which he has put is on palm oil. I am aware that the import of palm oil has had 
somewhat of a deleterious impact on the prices of

coconut oil particularly, in Kerala. But I would like to ask the hon. Member to bear in mind the 
fact that palm oil is imported into India because o f the fact that our domestic edible oil 
production is simply not suflficient to meet the increase in consumption. We are importing 
palm oil to meet the domestic demand. Palm oil is consumed all over the country. But coconut 
oil is consumed only in Kerala. And, my own experience is that a large number of consumers 
in Kerala prefer palm oil to coconut oil.

Industrial Corridor between Delhi and Mumbai  
†*285. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether scheme to build industrial corridor between Delhi and Mumbai with the 
partnership of India and Japan has been finalised; 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

 
12    Oral Answers  [RAJYA SABHA]  to Questions  
(b) if SO, detailed outline thereof; 
(c) the areas included in this Industrial Corridor between Delhi and Mumbai; and 
(d) the schemes formulated by Government for the development of these areas? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRIAL POLICY AND 
PROMOTION, MINISTRY OFCOMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRIASHWANI KUMAR): 
(a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) The Government of India has granted 'in-principle' approval to the development of 
Delhi and Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC) in August 2007. Inputs by an Indo-Japan Task 
Force set up under a MoU with the Government of Japan were also used to developing the' 
Project. 
(b) The approach of DMIC project is to provide good quality industrial infrastructure in 
selected industrial nodes. Industrial infrastructure will include industrial estates, knowledge 
hubs, agro processing hubs, IT/ITES hubs, logistics hubs and physical infrastructure (feeder 
roads/rail line, ports, airports, power etc.). An Apex Monitoring Authority has been constituted 
by the Government of India with 8 Central Ministers and Chief Ministers of UP, Haryana, 
Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra to provide overall guidance, planning 
and approvals. A corporate entity "Delhi Mumbai Industrial Corridor Development Corporation 
(DMICDC) with 49% equity by Government of India is envisaged for project development, co-
ordination and financing wherever needed. Phase I of the project is scheduled to be completed 
in synchronization with Delhi Mumbai Dedicated Rail Freight Corridor." 
(c) The Government has approved development of 12 industrial nodes in Uttar Pradesh, 
Haryana, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Maharashtra in the Phase I of the project 
as below:— 
Investment Regions (over 200 square kilometers):  
• Dadri-Noida-Ghaziabad Investment Region in Uttar Pradesh; 
• Manesar-Bawal Investment Region in Haryana; 
• Khushkhera-Bhiwadi-Neemrana Investment Region in Rajasthan; 
• Pitampura-Dhar-Mhow Investment Region in Madhya Pradesh; 
• Bharuch-Dahej Investment Region in Gujarat; 
• Igatpuri-Nashik-Sinnar Investment Region in Maharashtra. 
Industrial Areas (over IGO square Kilometers):  
• Meerut-Muzaffamagar Industrial Area in Uttar Pradesh. 
• Faridabad-PalwallndustrialArea in Haryana, 
• Jaipur-Dausa Industrial Area in Rajasthan, 
• Neemach Industrial Area in Madhya Pradesh, 
• Vadodara-Ankleshwar Industrial Area in Gujarat, 
• Alewadi/Dighi in Maharashtra.

SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, I would like to categorically assure the hon. Member that 
the in-principle approval of the project corridor has been given to the DMIC. In fact, when 
the Prime Minister of Japan visited India in August, the agreements were signed and were 
approved. And I am happy to inform the hon. Member that, according to our estimates, the 
work will begin early next year and the first phase of the project is likely to be completed by 
the year 2012. I am also happy to inform the hon. M ember that the Government is an 
advanced stage of short-listing the project management consultants who would be devising 
various specific schemes and projects that would be culled out of the master plans that are 
now in the process of being formulated. In the mean while, a three-tier structure has been 
established. One is the apex monitoring committee, which is chaired by the Finance Minister 
of India and it has eight Central Cabinet Ministers on it, six Chief Ministers of the concerned 
States through which the project will be executed. On the operational side, we are incorporating 
a company known as the Delhi-Mumbai Indistrial Corridor Corporation which will oversee 
the implementation of the various projects in assoc iation with the project management 
consultant. Sir, this project is a national project, the only project of its kind. It is estimated, as 
of now, that when completed, it would involve a capital outlay of close to a hundred billion 
dollars, about 90 billion dollars to be precise, or, Rs.3,60,000 crores. It would quadruple the 
employment and increase exports manifold and, that is why, it is receiving the top priority 
from the Government.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Shri Santosh Bagrodia. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Sir, the hon. Minister has mentioned twice; ones in the 
written reply and then again in reply to the earlier supplementary that Phase-I of the project 
is scheduled to be completed in synchronisation with Delhi- Mumbai Dedicated Rail Freight 
Corridor. Now, Sir, when we acquire land for Railways, that is a different situation. I would like 
to know from the hon. Minister whether we are acqui ring the same land which is actually 
acquired for railways, and now it will be used for industrialisation. If that is so, is it legally and 
technically right because we will be misguiding the  people of our nation that we have 
acquired it for a purpose and then we are using it for a different purpose. If not, who will 
acquire land? Sir, acquisition of land is a very big issue in the country today. Who will own 
this land? I am asking this question because 49 per cent is with the Government, I mean, this 
is all vague. I'would like the hon. Minister to please clarify as to who is going to control all 
this land along with the Delhi-Mumbai Dedicated Rail Freight Corridor. 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, I would like to inform the hon. Member that as far as land 
acquisition is concerned, the land that is specific ally acquired for establishing the Delhi-
Mumbai Rail Freight Corridor is one part of the story. The Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor 
is going to come up in an area of about 150 to 200 square kilometres on either side of the 
track, which would be a subject matter of separate acquisition. Now, Sir, the point that is 
important, and what the hon. Member asked is, what would be the ownership of the land. Sir, 
the ownership of the land will initially be vested in the acquiring authority, which, in the 
initial stages, could be the DMICDC. Although the government has directly 49 per cent in 
it, but the rest of the 51 per cent is going to be disbursed. Sir, that it will be with the FIIs, it 
will be with infrastructure development organisation like the IDFC, which again are primarily 
confrolled by the Government. So, depending upon the need, depending upon the extent of 
the acquisition required, Sir, the special purpose vehicles and the DMICDC will actually do 
that. But all of this, at this stage, is in a preli minary stage. As we go along the path of 
execution, we will find the best, the most appropriate and certainly the legal mechanisms to 
go in for the acquisition so that these are not stopped. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether it will 
be Government-controlled or private-controlled. 

Oral Answers  [5 DEC. 2007]  to Questions    15 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, as of now, the equity structure of the DMICDC says that 
49 percent will be directly held by the Government. The rest of the equity structure will be 
such that institutions in which the Government also  has majority control will be major 
participants. The exact contours of the equity structure have not been worked out. 
SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: Sir, I was interested in the earlier question, not in this one. 
SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, this Delhi-Mumbai industrial Corridor is going to be an 
important scheme of the Government, and the questio n asked by Shri Datta Meghe is an 
important one. In Maharashtra, the people of Vidarbha always feel that it is a backward area, 
there is no development in the area, and the people of Vidarbha have asked for a separate State 
also. Therefore, it becomes absolutely necessary that Vidarbha, which includes Nagpur also, 
becomes a part of this particular scheme. I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether 
the Government of Maharashtra has sent a proposal to the Government of India to include this 
particular area in this corridor. I would also like to know from the hon. Minister whether he 
would like to call the Members of Parliament from Vidarbha for a discussion in connection with 
this corridor. 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, I respect the sentiment of  hon. Joshiji. As far as 
development of Vidarbha region is concerned, we are  second to none in seeking to 
promote the all-round development of Vidarbha regio n. Sir, we have received three 
representations so far from the Chief Ministers of Tamil Nadu, from Punjab and from 
Gujarat. Sir, as far as I am aware, as on date, there is no proposal received specifically for 
getting the corridor extended to cover Vidarbha reg ion, Nagpur in particular. But, as I 
said. Sir, we have an open mind. If technically feasible, and if representations are received, 
we would, certainly, look at it with an open mind. The only difficulty. Sir, that we face, as 
far as including more and more areas in this system  is concerned, is that for it to be 
viable, it must be contiguous or close to the Rail Freight alignment. That is the only 
technical requirement. Subject to that, we have an open mind. Sir, we would be very 
happy to invite Members of Parliament from the regi on at any time and I would be 
available at your convenience to meet and discuss things. 
SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Sir, I would like to know from the hon. Minister the time-
frame within which the Master Plans would be ready, since he has not given the time-frame. 
In part (b) of the answer he has talked about the i nfrastructure of airports and power. 
Maharashtra already has a deficit of 5,500 MWs today. How are you going to address this 
problem? 
SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR: Sir, as far as the Master Plan's time-frame is concerned, we 
are still at the stage of short-listing and hiring a project management consultant who will 
then be working with the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Co rridor Corporation Management to 
find out what are the best linkages that could be i dentified and then the work would start. 
As far as linkages and connectivity are concerned, the answer is in the context of what 
will be the contribution of the Central Government. We have said that the State Governments, 
the Central Government, the stake-holders, the deve lopers, the Special Purpose Vehicle 
would all pool in their resources. The Central Gove rnment would assist in creating the 
necessary physical infrastructure consisting of rail linkages, ports, power, etc. etc. 
As far as the availability of certain infrastructure in Maharashfra is concerned, 
none doubts that. I said earlier and I would like to repeat it, that as far as including more

areas in this project is concerned, that is a function of its viability and synchronisation with 
the alignment of the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor Corporation.

Separate labour laws for SEZs  
*284. SHRI MAHENDRAMOHAN: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government intends to have separate labour laws for Special 
Economic zones (SEZs); 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the kind of changes contemplated in the existing labour laws; 
(c) whether Government has consulted the various stakeholders in this r« vd; 
(d) how labour disputes are currently dealt with in the existing set up; 
(e) whether Government has received any representations in this regard; and 
(f) if so, what kind of dispute settlement mechanism has been desired by the workers in the 
SEZs? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMALNATH): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Do not arise. 
(d) to (f) In the Special Economic zones (SEZs) where the Development Commissioners 
(DCs) of the Zones are declared as 'Labor Commissio ners' by the respective State 
Governments, the DCs exercise the same dispute resolution mechanism as exercised by the State 
Government Labour Officers. While the State Labour Department officials are also 
consulted/involved in case of major disputes, minor disputes are resolved in the zone through 
consultations with the DC of the Zone and his staff  Representations suggesting that there 
should not be any dilution of workers' rights in th e Special Economic Zones (SEZs) were 
received. 
Extension of NREGS  
*286.      SHRI DARA SINGH: 
SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 

24    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Starred Questions  
(a) whether Government proposes to extend the National Rural Employment Guarantee 
Scheme (NREGS) all over the country; 
(b) if so, whether ground work to extend the scheme has been completed; 
(c) the fund earmarked for the purpose; 
(d) the number of additional families likely to be covered under NREGS; 
(e) whether any suggestion/request has come from States in this regard; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (DR. RAGHUVANSH PRASAD SINGH): (a) 
and (b) Yes, Sir. Govenunent of India has decided to extend NREGS to all the remaining rural 
districts in the country, including the Union Territories with effect from 1.4.2008. A notification 
to this effect was issued on 28.9.2007. A sum of Rs. 159.44 crore have been released to the 
Phase III districts (except districts of Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat) for making preparatory 
arrangements like lEC, printing and procurement of statutory documents, training of officials and non-
officials and preparation of perspective plans. 
(c) NREGA is demand driven and not an allocation based programme. A National 
Employment Guarantee Fund has been established for providing funds to the States for 
implementation of the Act. For the current financial year, a budget provision of Rs. 12,000 crores 
was made for implementation of the Act. Provisions are made in the budget for implementation 
of the Act on the basis of frinds utilized by the States and also on the basis of demand for work 
in the previous year. 
(d) NREGA is demand driven. Adult members of any rural household may apply for 
employment under the Act subject to an over-all cei ling of 100 days of employment in a 
financial year per household. Therefore, no targets can be fixed for providing employment under 
the Act. 
(e) and (f) Suggestions/requests had been received from various States for coverage of 
selected districts under NREGA. However, Government has decided to extend NREGA to all the 
remaining rural districts in the country including Union Territories with effect from 1.4.2008.

Construction of roads in Buxar under PMGSY  
*289. SHRI BASHISTHANARAIN SINGH: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the details of roads being constructed under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) 
in the Buxar district of Bihar; 
(b) their completion schedule, funds allocated and percentage of completion of work so far; 
(c) is there any time and cost overrun; 
(d) the details of the roads proposed to be taken in the next fmancial year; 
(e) the proposed time-limit for the completion of Itarhi-Koran Sarai segment; 
(f) whether there is any complaint from the public regarding quality of work; and 
(g) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTEROF RURAL  DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD SINGH): (a) 
Under Phase I of PMGSY, 4 nos. road works were sanctioned for Buxar district of Bihar and have 
been completed. Under Phase II, 16 nos. road works were sanctioned out of which 14 have been 
completed. The details have been given in statement I (See below). The details of road works 
taken up from Phase III onwards have been given in Statement II. (See below). 
(b) Programme guidelines stipulate that all works should be completed within 12 months from 
the date of issue of work order. Details of sanctioned cost and physical progress have been given 
in Statement I & II (See below). 
(c) There is no cost overrun. There Is timed overrun du e to Panchayat elections, 
encroachment, rainy season etc.

agencies to the Ministry, the proposals are scrutinized and accorded clearance. All efforts are

Estimated loss of crops and people in Bihar due to floods 
1686. SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the estimated loss caused to the farmers, standing crops and people of Bihar due to 
recent heavy floods; 
(b) whether any relief has been given to the flood affected people and if so, to whom and 
how much and the details thereof. District-wise and 
(c) the number of houses of poor people that have been damaged and is there any 
proposal to construct new houses for them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V. 
RADHIKA SELVI): (a) to (c) According to the memorandum submitted by the Government 
ofBihar for floods of 2007, 16.40 lakh hectares of cropped area & about 5.12 lakh houses 
have been damaged, besides loss of 510 human lives and 559 cattle heads in 9939 villages 
covering 20 districts. 
In the wake of natural calamities, the concerned State Governments are primarily 
responsible to distribute relief on ground. The Central Government supplements the efforts 
of the State Governments by providing financial and  logistic support. A Calamity Relief 
Fund (CRF) has been constituted for such State base d on the recommendations of the 
successive Finance Commissions. The corpus of CRF is contributed by the Government of 
India and the State Government in the ratio of 75:2 5. The Central Share is released in two 
equal installment — first in June and second in Dec ember. Additional Central Assistance is 
also provided in the wake of a calamity of severe nature from National Calamity Contingency 
Fund (NCCF), after following the laid-down procedure. 
The State Government had undertaken rescue and relief operations in the affected areas 
which include operation of relief camps and providing essential commodities viz. air dropped 
71000 readymade food packets weighing 355 tons, distributed about 58000 MT wheat & rice 
as well as 10559 quintals of dry ration (Chura, sat tu, salt, etc), 2 lakh pieces of candles, 
1.50 lakh match-boxes and 2.63 lakh polythene sheets. In addition, Rs 3231.00 lakh was also 
reportedly distributed as cash doles. 
Bihar has been allocated an amount of Rs. 157.74 cr ore in CRF for the year 2007-08 
consisting of Rs. 118.31 crore as Central contribution and Rs. 39.43 crore as State contribution. 
Both the installments of Central share of CRF amounting of Rs. 59.155 crore each, have been 
released to the State Government, including advance  release of 2nd installment of Central 
share. In addition, an amount of Rs. 114.92 crore has also been released as pending Central 
share of CRF for the year 2006-07. 
Based on the request of the State Government, the Government of India made additional 
allocation of 2.00 lakh MT of rice & 1.00 lakh MT of wheat & 10,000 KL of kerosene oil to 
Bihar. Transportation of fodder by rail from Punjab to the affected districts in Bihar was also 
organized by Government of India at no cost to the State Government. 
According to its memorandum, the State Government has proposed to construct 4.8 lakh 
houses under the Scheme of Indira Awas Yojana (lAY) for those Below Poverty Line (BPL) 
families whose houses have been damaged during the floods of 2007.

in the denomination of Rs. 500 and 203 counterfeit notes in the denomination of Rs. 1000 were

which inter-alia include sharing of intelligence with the State Gove rnment; sharing up of 
vigilance by the Border Security Force/Customs authorities to prevent smuggling of fake currency 
notes into the country; dissemination of information on security features through print and

PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA:

Ministers' meeting was held in New Delhi and decided to set up an institutional mechanism to 
enhance cooperation among SAARC Nations to meet the growing challenge of terrorism in the 
region;

people? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRIMATI V.

putting in place effective measures to control the activities of various militants groups. The 
steps taken in this regard inter-alia, incldue deployment of Central Security Forces, including 
Army, to assist the State police, sharing of intelligence, provision of assistance to the State 
Government for strengthening and modernization of the local police, raising of India Reserve 
Battalions, reimbursement of security related expenditure to the State Government etc. The 
situation is being reviewed and monitored on a regular basis.

Code of conduct for Media Reporting  
1726. DR. K. KESHAVA RAO: Will the Minister of INFO RMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Press Council of India, at its recent meeting recommended the 
constitution of regulatory body to frame a code of conduct to check distortions in media reporting; 
(b) what steps is the Government taking to bring electronic media under the purview of the 
Press Council of India; 
(c) whether Government is also contemplating to bring measures to contain the increased fake 
sting operations by the electronic media; and 
(d) what steps the Government is envisaging to ensure media accountability? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI PRIYARANJAN 
DASMUNSI): (a) and (b) The Chairman, Press Council of India, requested the Govenunent vide his letter 
dated 20th September 2006 for establishment of a common authority for content regulation of the 
media and preservation of its freedom by extending the jurisdiction of Press Council over electronic as 
well as print media and renaming it MEDIA MONITORING COMMISSION OF INDIA. The request 
was examined but, it was not found possible to accede to the proposal. 
(c) and (d) The Government is conmiitted to the freedom of press in the print media. It follows a 
policy of non-interference in the affairs of the print media. The Goverrmient has set up the Press 
Council of India which looks into complaints against the print media. 
In case of the electronic media, the TV channels are autonomous and there is no proposal to curb 
their autonomy. However, they have to abide by the Programme and Advertising Code as 
prescribed under Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 and rules framed thereunder 
and any other regulation issued from time to time. Any violation of these Codes is dealt with under 
the relevant rules. A Committee has also been constituted for reviewing the existing Programme 
and Advertising Codes prescribed under the Cable TV Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 and rules 
framed thereunder and the guidelines for certification of films prescribed under Cinematography 
Act, 1952 and for drafting a new content Code. Latest formulation of the draft prepared by this 
Conunittee which, inter alia, deals with privacy issues/sting operations, is avai lable at 
www.mib.nic.in . Consultations which the stakeholders are continuing.

combination of Cash and in-kind. Thus, 67% of employed women in the age group 15 to 49 earn

for the same work or work of a similar nature without any discrimination. This Act is implemented

compliance of the provisions of the Act. For the areas under the Central Government, the Act is

working conditions for women employed and to prevent their exploitation. These include the 
Factories Act, 1948, the Plantation Labour Act, 1951, the Contract Labour (Regulation and 
Abolition) Act, 1970, the Inter-State Migrant Worke rs (Regulation of Employment and 
Conditkns of Service) Act, 1979, the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, the Buildings and Other 
Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996, 
Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 etc. >%4iich provide inter-alia, creche facilities for the benefit of 
women workers, time off for the feeding children du ring working hours, provision of 
maternity leave and separate toilets and washing facilities for female and male workers near 
the workplace as well as safe working conditions.

night shift in the factories etc. provided the empl oyer makes adequate arrangements for 
their safety and security, is under consideration in the Parliament. 
(c) The existing provisions of laws and practices a re adequate for this purpose.

National Poilcy on Rehabilitation and Resettlement, 2007  
1755. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI : Will the Minister o f RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT  be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact Government have approved the N ational Policy on 
Rehabilitation and Resettlement (R&R) 2007, to repl ace the National Policy on 
Rehabilitation and Resettlement for Project Affected Families, 2003; 
(b) if so, details in this regard; 
(c) how the social assessment impact will be assessed under the new policy; 
(d) whether under this policy without settlement, displacement will not be done; and 
(e) whether the new policy takes into consideration cul tural ethos and idigenous right 
of adivasis? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVE LOPMENT 
(SHRI CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. T he National Rehabilitation 
and Resettlement Policy, 2007 formulated by this Mi nistry has been approved by the 
Cabinet and has come into force w.e.f. 31 st October, 2007, the date of its publication in  
the Gazette of India (Extraodinary). This policy re places the earlier policy, the National 
Policy on Resettlement & Rehabilitation for Project  Affected Families, 2003. The policy 
document is also available at the websites of the M inistry of Rural Development  Error! 
Hyperlink reference not valid.) and the Development of Land Resources {http://dolr . 
nic.in).  
The policy provides for the basic minimum requireme nts that must be met by all 
projects leading to involuntary displacement of peo ple, while the State Governments, 
Public Sector Undertakings or agencies, and other r equiring bodies may put in place 
greater benefits levels than those prescribed. The principles of the policy may also apply 
to the rehabilitation and resettlement of persons i nvoluntary displaced permanently due 
to any other reason. 
(c) The policy emhpasizes that whenever it is desir ed to undertake a new project or 
expansion of an existing project, which involves in voluntary displacement of four 
hundred or more families en masse in plain areas, or two hundred or more families en 
masse in tribal or hilly areas, DDP blocks or areas menti oned in Schedule V or Schedule 
VI to the Constitution, the appropriate Govenunent shall ensure that a Social Impact 
Assessment (SIA) study is carried out in the propos ed affected areas in such manner as 
may be prescribed. 

170    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
(d) The policy has highlighted that in case of a project involving land acquisition on behalf of 
a requiring body, the compensation award shall be declared well in time before displacement of the 
affected families. Full payment of compensation as well as adequate progess in resettlement shall 
be ensured in advance of the actual displacement of the affected families. 
(e) The policy document has also emphasized that the Scheduled Tribes affected families 
will be re-settled, as far as possible, in the same Schedule Area in a compact block, so that they can 
retain their ethnic, linguistic and cultural identity.

1766. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of RU RAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether under the on-going Swamjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana, credit-linked self 
employment programmes are under.implementation; 
(b) if so, how many self help groups have been formed under the SGSY and the amount of 
funds disbursed as credit to Swarozgaris during the last year; and 
(c) to what extent the proposed Micro-finance Bill, when enacted, is likely to ensure credit 
flow to self-employed in rural areas? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
CHANDRASEKHAR SAHU): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Number of Self Help Groups formed during 2006-07 were 245090 under the SGSY, 
Credit Target were Rs. 286912.31 lacs and Credit Disbursed were Rs. 227608.34 (79.33%) A 
Statement is given (See below). 
(c) The Government has introduced a bill in Lok Sabha on 20.03.2007 "The Micro Financial Sector 
(Development and Regulation) Bill, 2007" to create environment friendly policy for micro-
finance services in the country. The bill is intended to provide formal statutory framework for 
the promotion, development and regulation of the micro fmance sector. The salient features of 
this bill are follows:— 
(i)    entrusts the function of development and regulation of the micro fmancial sector to 
the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (National Bank); 
(ii) defines the various entities engaged in the ac tivity of micro fmance such as 
Cooperative Societies, etc.; 
(iii) defines the various categories of beneficiaries of micro fmancial services as eligible

Effect of Import of thread and raw material from China as cottage industry 
† 1784. SHRI ALI ANWAR: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps being taken by Government to save the  cottage industry of Indian weavers 
which is in a miserable condition due to import of thread and raw material from China at a 
cheaper rate; 
(b) whether Government are aware that our weavers are facing terrible crises due to import 
of thread and raw material from China at a cheaper rate; and 
(c) the initiatives being taken by Government to provide loans to weavers at low rates of 
interest? 
THE MINISTEROF STATE INTHEMINISTRYOFTEXnLES(SHRI E.V.K.S.  ELANGOVAN): 
(a) and (b) The Central Silk Board has taken the initiative to file petitions with the Director 
General of Antidumping and Allied Duties for imposition of antidumping duty on the cheap 
imports of raw silk and silk fabrics from China to safeguard the interest of the domestic 
sericulture & silk industry. The antidumping duty on the import of raw silk of 2A and below is 
in place and will be in force till January 2008. The Central Silk Board has initiated the process 
for continuation of this antidumping duty for a further period of 5 years by filing the Sunset 
Review Petition. Similarly, the antidumping duty on the import of silk fabrics is in place from 
November 2006, which will be in force till 2011. 
(c) To address issues relating to credit to the handloom sector, a meeting was held under 
the Chairmanship of Secretary (Textiles) and it was  decided to constitute a Committee 
comprising the MD, NABARD, as Convenor and Represen tatives of Indian Banking 
Association (1BA)/Reserve Bank of India (RBI)/National Institute of Fashion Technology 
(NIFT)/Secretary (Handlooms), Government of Orissa/ Tamil Nadu/Uttar Pradesh/Assam/ 
Kerala/Kamataka/West Bengal/Andhra Pradesh and representative of National Association 
of State Cooperative and Additional Development com missioner for Handlooms. The 
Committee had submitted the total budget for implementation of Handloom Weavers' Financial 
Package for Handloom for Rs. 1295 crore, which comprise shares of Government of India, 
State Government and contribution from NABARD. The financial Package proposal was 
sent to the Ministry of Finance, which had inter-alia, suggested that State Government 
bear the large share of responsibility. The CNE not e in this regard was circulated to the 
Ministry of Finance. Planning Commission and Prime Minister's Office. The Ministry of 
Finance has advised to rework the proposal incorpor ating their suggestion for framing the 
proposal for Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA).

SHRI BALAVANT/lI/^5 BAL APTE: Sir, I rise to give my views on this Bill, which, in the ultimate 
analysis, will be a good effort. But, the process, through which it has gone, painfully realises that this 
Government does not mean honest business. Sir, we need institute of excellence in medicine 
both for teaching and public service throughout the country. When the matter arose the other day, 
we were told that we could establish institutes only in Union Territories and nowhere else. But, the 
fact remains that entry 64 gives ample scope to the  Central Government to establish such 
institutions throughout the country. In fact, the earlier Government had proposed to have six such 
institutes of excellence throughout the country which will give education as well as render 
effective public service in matters of medical treatment. For reasons best known to them, the 
present Government abandoned that excellent scheme, as it had tended to do with several other 
schemes and for the first three years of its governance, the country has suffered. The schemes for 
infrastructure development, for development of roads, for inter-linking of rivers, which were taking 
people on the road of progress, were halted irrationally in a manner which was totally partisan and, 
therefore, did not go with national interest. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN, (PROF. P.J. KURIEN), in the Chair.] 
The establishment of the institutes also had the sa me fate. But now, probably the 
Government has woken up to the need for establishment of such institutes, and, therefore, has 
sought. ...(Interruptions).. Sir, in an empty House, I must, at least, have your attention. 
The establishment of this institute, which was already there since 1964 as a statutory body, 
under the aegis of the Central Government, maybe with assured fmancial support, is sought by this 
Bill. Insofar as incorporation of this institute and its governance is concerned, the objects talk about 
academic autonomy and then the proposal shows that the autonomy which is termed to be 
academic will be illusory if the present structure is permitted to hold. Sir, 

Government [5 DEC. 2007] Bills   237 
autonomy is not something which can be confined to detennination of courses, particularly, in 
a medical institute where you train doctors and you  render simultaneously excellent 
medical service to the people at large, particularl y, to the have-nots.Therefore, talking of 
academic autonomy is hollow if the institution is n ot fully autonomous. If you treat the full 
autonomy of an institute of medical education in a manner in which it ought not have to be 
done, every institute in the country will suffer th e same tragedy as the All India Institute of 
Medical Sciences in New Delhi has suffered during the last one year or more. 
Sir, the institutes cannot depend upon the whims and  fancies of the powers that be, 
particularly the Health Minister. They are not run by the persons whom he likes; and the 
persons whom he dislikes should not be removed. 
This Bill guarantees one more empire to the Ministe r for Health to deal casually with 
personnel, to deal casually with dignified people, and to deal casually with persons who 
have medical excellence but who are poor in subserving him. 
The attempt in the All India Institute of Medical S ciences by the Health Minister is a 
pointer to which this Government will tend to go, will stoop to go, to hamper both autonomy 
and service. 1, therefore, believe that the present institute will also suffer the same tragedy as 
the institute in Delhi is suffering. 
Sir, I had the privilege of reading the report of the Committee on this headed by Shri Amar 
Singh. It has also pointed out that this autonomy is very important. They, in fact, recommended in 
this Bill that the Minister should not be a Member of the Institute and should not be an ex 
officio President. The Bill provided this. Fortunate ly, some wisdom has dawned and they 
have removed the inclusion of the Minister. But the Secretary is very much there. 
Therefore, Sir, my first submission before you is t hat the concept of autonomy is not 
merely determining courses; the concept of autonomy  includes the administration of the 
institution, particularly because it is at the same  time a teaching institution as well as an 
institution for public service. This autonomy has t o be ensured. After the Report of the 
Standing Committee, the amendments, which are sought to be made here, are, in a way, very 
cosmetic. Only one clause is changed. 
Therefore, I would urge upon the Government to go back on this Bill and bring a Bill which will 
establish an autonomous institution of excellence which this country needs. 
In so far as the administrative autonomy is concern ed, it always depends upon the 
finances which an institution gets. Those who pay t he piper, they say, call the tune.That 
should not be the situation. The financial support to the institutions should be granted and 
the Ministry has only that role to play. The Ministry cannot determine things, and therefore, to 
ensure this autonomy, the appointment of persons on the Governing Body, the appointment of 
the Director, should be through a process which wil l ensure that that autonomy is fully 
protected. 
Secondly, Sir, in so far as the functioning of the Institute is concerned, the employees, the 
staff and the students are the essential part of an  institution. In fact, if an institution is 
academic, then the student is at the centre of the institution. Today, if the administration 
does not think about the welfare of |he students an d the staff, particularly in a medical 
institution, the residents, then the administration  goes haywire, the interests suffer, the 
institute suffers, the students suffer, and the public suffers. Therefore, it is imperative that 

238    Government [RAJYA SABHA] Bills  
these interests are represented in the administration. Participation is really the gravamen of 
any democracy, of any governance, and therefore, I would urge that the governance of this 
Institute should include the representatives of the employees, the staff and the students. Sir, 
my submission to this House is that unless you do it, time and again, there will be disruption in 
the activities. The resident doctors have genuine g rievances, and those grievances are 
never addressed unless they go on strike, and if they go on strike, then it is a step against the 
people, because a medical doctor is considered to be a God, and therefore, they suffer both 
ways. The people are against them and the administr ation is against them. All over the 
country, in so far as public hospitals are concerne d, the resident doctors work much more 
than what they are paid for. I know in most of thes e hospitals, the resident doctors work 
almost for 24 hours continuously. They are always on 24 hours duty, and they are not looked 
after, and a time comes when they consolidate and agitate. If this particular malady is to be 
addressed, I would urge that they should be represe nted effectively in the management so 
that they will be responsible and their grievances will also be addressed. With these, I would 
suggest that the Government should not proceed with  this Bill without making proper 
amendments. Thank you.

Situation arising out of misuse of funds provided by central 
government under national rural employment guarantee programme 
SHRl V. NARAYANASAMY (Puducherry): Sir, 1 would like to raise here a very important 
subject. Earlier, on several occasions, in the form of questions and Short Duration discussion, 
the issue of misuse of Employment Guarantee Scheme Funds by various States has been 
raised in this august House. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA) in the Chair.] 
Sir, day in and day out, there are reports from NGOs and from some independent bodies 
that the funds meant for National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme are being misused in 
this country. Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, it is a very important subject. The UPA Government in the 
Common Minimum Programme has clearly indicated that there should be job opportunity to 
the poor people living in the villages because urban people are getting employment with the 
infrastructure industry, service industry and with other industries. But people in the rural 
areas, the farm labours, when there is offseason, are not able to get employment and they 
have to sit idle at home and their families suffer and starve. Therefore, the UPA Government 
under the leadership of hon. Prime Minister and also the UPA Chairperson, the hon. Congress 
President, initiated the move, which was supported by all our alliance, that there should be 
job guarantee for the rural people provided by the Government themselves. Therefore, the 
scheme was implemented by the Government about two years back. Funds were provided. 
The salient feature of the Scheme is that in the ru ral areas, Adivasi people, the Scheduled 
Castes people, backward classes people, farm labour and the people who are not employed 
will get employment for 100 days in a year. And, the minimum wages should be paid at the 
rate of Rs.80 — in some of the States, it varies. —  and that employment should be provided 
to one member of the family, either male or female member; one family — one job. Under that 
Scheme, the funds were provided by the Central Governmenf to the States. Ninety per cent 
is the Central Government's share and ten per cent is the State Government's share. The job 
card is to be issued by the State Government to the poor people. On the basis of job card, the 
Gram Panchayat will give employment opportunity to them. The funds are given by the State 
Governments at the Gram Panchayat level, Tehsil lev el and also at the District level. The 
District Collector is the monitoring authority. That is the Scheme which is being implemented 
and it has got a wide welcome from the people of this country. Crores of unemployed people 
got employment and for one member in each family, p rovision was also made under the 
National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme that 33 per cent of the beneficiaries should be 
women. Out of the total persons given employment, 33 per cent ladies should be employed 
in rural areas. This is a very noble scheme, accept ed by the people of this country, 
l/nplementation has been made in various States. Sir, whatever money was required by the 
State Government on the basis ofenrolment made, the Central Government sent the money. 
But, unfortunately, at the State level, at the implementation stage, there is lot of corruption, 
mismanagement, misuse of funds. The jobs are not being given as per the guidelines issued 
by the Government of India. We have raised this issue several tmics. Rur. Sir, in this country', in 
the Northern part of the country, there are tribal peop'e and the tribal people live in

minimum of Rs.6000 to Rs.8000 per month which is going to sustain the whole  family if the

the Scheme was launched by the hon. Prime Minister and hon. Chairperson of the UPA from

SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: Sir, I have mentioned the Katni district in Madhya Pradesh. Even after 
the work is being done by those poor people, for 15 days, 20 days, 6 months, wages are not 
paid to them, and they have to wait to get their wager. The Government of India has given the 
money. What is the problem for the State and the districts in distributing the money to the deserving 
people? Therefore, I want the hon. Minister to have a foolproof mechanism to monitor it. It should 
not be used for the purpose of furthering the interest of any political party. It should be for the poor 
people, the laudable object with which the UPA Government has brought this scheme. Secondly, 
when there is corruption and misuse of funds, take action against them. Tell the State 
Governments to take action against them. Rs. 100 crores have been siphoned off in the Katni 
district so far, no action has been taken so far, in Chhattisgarh no action has been taken. 
Today also a lot of questions have been raised on the NREG Programme. The hon. Prime 
Minister has very clearly stated that the Government is prepared to give any amount of money 
that the State Governments want for providing jobs to the poor people. It is the guarantee that 
the hon. Prime Minister has given here. On the request of our young leader, the Prime Minister 
said that we would extend it throughout the country in

April, 2008. Earlier it was implemented in 200 distri cts. It has been increased to 350 
districts. Now, we are going to have it throughout the country. I am grateful to the hon. 
Minister for doing this. But as regards implementati on, there is a lot of lacuna, misuse, 
mismanagement and corruption. I want the hon. Minis ter to consider all these. I feel the 
only mechanism by which you can do it is to monitor  it through the public representatives, 
instead of officials. That is the only solution whi ch I could find. You are holding meetings. 
You should hold meetings, at least, once in three m onths to review the working and 
spending, and to see whether the right people have been given the jobs. It should be 
found out so that corruption, mismanagement and misuse of funds can be eliminated. The 
hon. Minister is capable of doing it. He has taken action in certain States where it has 
been misused. But there is large scale misuse of fun ds. I want" the hon. Minister to take 
strict action and to appoint a monitoring committee , not at the administrative level but of 
the people who have got experience in the field. It  should be monitored through it so that 
the funds will go to the poor people and the poor p eople, who deserve it, will get 
employment. 
With these observations, I request the hon. Minister to take immediate action in this 
regard. Thank you.

THE MINISTEROF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): Sir, I 
would like to bring to the notice of the House certain facts about the JIPMER Bill. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIEN): So, you are speaking on the Bill. 
DR. ANBUMANI RAMDOSS: Sir, I just want to explain somethi ng. By taking this 
opportunity. Sir, I wish to explain the situation ab out this Bill. There are a number of 
observations made by the hon. Members. 1 am happy to reply the same. As mentioned in the 
Bill, the JIPMER is an institute of national importanc e. The JIPMER, AIIMS and PGl, 
Chandigarh are the three institutes set up more tha n fifty years ago which envisages as a 
centre of excellence. The PGI, Chandigarh and the AIIMS, at that point of time, were made as a 
centre of excellence through an Act of Parliament and the JIPMER was left out. There were a 
lot of Committees which, at that point of time, in the early 60s, recommended that the 
JIPMER should also be made as a centre of excellence under an Act of Parliament. Even after 
fifty years, none of the observation/recommendation s of Committees was implemented. 
There has been a lot of activity in the Institute. I will answer all the queries raised by the hon. 
Members. Sir, even though I was bom in Puducherry and this Institute is there in Puducherry, 
as a doctor, as a professional myself, I know how t he Institute has been fiinctioning in the 
last 25 years. Sir, it was a centre of excellence at one point of time and if you see the graph, it 
came down. The efficiency, functioning of the Institute came down. Mr. Narayanasamy was 
saying that there is no neurologist in the Institute. Since the last 3'/^ years, after the UPA 

Government [5 DEC. 2007] Bills   265 
Government had taken over, now, we have been trying  to restructure the Institute. There 
have been administrative problems earlier. People were asking why it should be made as an 
autonomous. Some people are asking why it should not be made autonomous. So, there is a 
little confusion. On the one hand, some people want autonomy, and, on the other, people do 
not want autonomy. I do not know which way to follo w. On some issues, people very 
strongly say that autonomy should be maintained and there should not be any interference 
with its autonomy and here we are trying to give autonomy to the Institute and some of them 
are opposing for the reasons best known to them. 
So, I am not able to understand this duplicity of policies. This institute, geographically, is in 
the Southern-most part of the country. We have institutes, like, the Safdarjang Hospital, the 
RML Hospital and the JIPMER, which come under the Central Health Service. The PGIMR 
and the AIIMS come under the statute. Since it is in the Southern most part of the country, a 
lot of activities do not happen there. Even though t here have been fmancial allocations to 
the institute, but these have not been fully observ ed. And, as hon. Narayanasamy has 
said, "When you think of putting any query or writing letters, one year is done." Here, in the 
RML Hospital and the Safdarjang Hospital, accessibility of officers is there to get the things 
done then and there. But due to geographical reasons , there are no functions, nothing 
happens. Then, there is another component of the programme, that is, the appointments by 
the UPSC. The UPSC takes one to two years to comple te the appointment procedure, 
interviews, etc., and appoint a doctor. Then, half of the doctors do not join because of the 
geographical famess. And, those who join, they want transfer to Delhi or in the Northern part 
of the country. Because of this, nearly 50-60 per c ent vacancies were lying vacant in the 
JIPMER, before we took over. And, what to say, even the CT machine, though it was a new 
one, was not functioning there. After I took over, within a span of one week the scan machine 
started functioning. So, such was the state of affair. 
Incidentally, I, the Minister, happen to be from th at part of the country. Things are 
happening. We are giving more allocation and concentration to that. But I am not going to be 
here permanently. As Shrimati Brindaji was saying, there were, cutting across the party lines, a 
lot of animosity or the agitations. I would like to  state that the major parties in Puducherry 
have supported this proposal. The major parties, who are ruling there, who have the maximum 
MLAs and MPs, have supported this proposal of providi ng autonomy. We have gone into 
the pros and cons of the issue. We had series of discussions. I myself had discussions with 
the employees and with other parties. My officers h ad so many discussions. My Secretary 
had discussions. Members of Parliament, both, from the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, had 
discussions with them. There were some apprehension s too. But saying that the entire 
institute opposes it, is not completely true. Almost  all the doctors and all the categories of 
staff want this autonomy. I have been getting so many letters that they wanted this statute, 
for a long time, for its improvement, for its academic excellence, for it to have its own curriculum. 
The JIPMER students are there all over the world, and  wherever I would go, they would 
insist that there should be a statute because no institute, no hospital can function with 50-60 
per cent of posts lying vacant. Till about two year s ago, there was no Neurologist. If any 
accident victim would go there, they would refer him to the Government Hospital, Puducherry. 
And, this was supposed to be a centre of excellence!  But, nothing was happening. That's 
why we need a statute; we need a governing body to function within the rules of Parliament. 
And, we are all willing to support the financial component. 
Sir, Mr. Narayanasamy is right in saying that patients, from all over the country go there.

He was also saying that funds were not being proper ly utilized earlier. But we have been 
taking a lot of measures and steps to streamline the administrative functioning and sort out 
the various problems. We are trying to focus on providing better patient care and all that. He 
also said that reservation policy was to be safegua rded. Definitely, it is the policy of the 
Government to safeguard the reservation policy of t he JIPMER in Puducherry. The poor 
patients will be treated free of cost. It is definitely the policy of the UPA Government, whether it 
is the AIIMS or the PGIMR or any other institution, run by the Government of India, to treat all 
poor people free of cost. And, we are treating them  totally free of cost. We don't charge 
them. And, it is not only for Below the Poverty Line patients only, but, even for poor patients 
who say that we cannot afford and we are treating t hem. It is not that when it becomes a 
statute, the costs are going to be increased. Definitely, it is not going to be increased. 
There was a suggestion that the fee structure of th e students should not be altered. I 
would like to assure Smt. Brinda Karat that the fee  structure for the students will not be 
altered. But, then, as she wants, I don't think there is any Act, which says that the present fee 
structure should be protected. It cannot be mentioned in any Act. I am willing to mention it in 
the rules as such. As an Administrator, she also knows and all the Members of Parliament 
know that this present clause for which she has mov ed an amendment cannot be brought 
under the Bill per se. It could be brought under the rules. The rules could be changed then 
and there, but not the Bill, which she wants to be done. 
About allocation of funds, I would like to assure M r. Narayanasamy that all the funds 
necessary to upgrade are being given. In fact, last year, we had given nearly about Rs. 180 
crores upgradation and we are trying to do that. We have given even more than that. He also 
mentioned about employees. Yes, Sir, we have given employees one-year time to choose 
whether they want to be in the present structure or  move to the newer structure. All the 
departments related to heart surgery, orthopaedic etc., definitely, all these will be taken care 
of 
My colleague, the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Health, Shri Amar Singhji was 
telling us about poor patients. Definitely, poor pa tients will be taken care of. This is an 
assurance from the Government. He was also asking a bout the Standing Committee's 
recommendations. He also knows that most of the rec ommendations of the Standing 
Committee have been accepted and incorporated. All the hon. Members know about it. 
Definitely, we have to work in tandem. Both the Ministry as well as the Standing Committee on 
Health are working and will work in tandem. 
Sir, I have already replied to Smt. Brinda Karat about the agitation and the objective. We 
are also willing to accept the amendment, which she is bringing with the objective to continue 
to provide patient care delivery services free of c ost for poor patients. Definitely, we are 
willing to concede to that to bring it under the Bill. 
About the fee structure, I have already mentioned. Smt. Brinda Karat said that it should be 
brought under the Bill. Definitely, legally and administratively also, I don't think there is such an

like.

SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, Sir, for  allowing me to take 
part in the discussion on the National Rural Employ ment Guarantee Scheme. As we all 
know, the Scheme was fu^t introduced in 200 district s with a lot of fanfare, later extended 
to 137 more 

Short Duration [5 DEC. 2007] Discussion   277 
districts and, now, it has been extended to the who le of India. It has started, initially, in 19 
districts in my State of Andhra Pradesh. The NREG Act, 2 005 provides enhancement of 
livelihood security by giving, at least, 100 days o f guaranteed wage employment in every 
year to every household, whose adult members volunt eer to do unskilled manual work. 
Panchayats at districts, intermediate and village-l evels will be the principal authorities for 
planning and implementation of the scheme. Up to he re, everything sounds well. But, the 
problem starts thereafter. Sir, NREGS is a Central Scheme. But, unfortunately, many States are 
canvassing and implementing the Scheme as the State Scheme. And, it is not out of place to 
mention that my State is in the forefront in this. It has notified this Scheme as a State Scheme 
with the name AP Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme and issued the notification the very 
day the GOI issued the notification, that is, on February 2, making it as a Stale Scheme, not 
the Central Scheme. The misuse of the Scheme has started right from the day one. So, the first 
point I wish to make is that there has to be a dire ctive from the Government of India and 
propagate the same extensively by saying that this Scheme is being implemented by the 601, 
not the States. They are only the implementing agenc ies. The other point is, one of the 
guidelines of the Scheme says that men and women sh ould get equal pay. This provision, 
openly, hit for a six by every State and discriminate against women. Women are not getting 
the same amount as that of men. So I demand that equal pay should be ensured to women as 
well. 
Sir, the second point I wish to make is that m.any people in villages are not aware of this 
programme. There is lack of awareness among the poor people that the Government is doing 
something for them and they can reap the benefit of it. But, due to lack of awareness about 
this wage-employment programme, the purpose of the Scheme is defeated. This becomes 
clear if you look at the utilization of the scheme. So far, under the NREGS, only SO per cent of 
the funds have been utilised. So, there is a need to generate awareness through radio, local 
cultural resources, inter-personal communication, door-to-door contact campaigns, TV, etc. It 
is only then the Scheme percolate to the beneficiary . Otherwise, the contractors create 
duplicate pay-rolls and grab the money as is being done in almost all the districts where this 
scheme is being implemented. So, I suggest that to maintain the quality work, 60:40 ratio 
should be maintained for wages and material. 
Sir, the next point I wish to touch upon and is also today's main point of the discussion is 
misuse of funds. For this, I would say that there needs to be transparency in selection and 
designing of works undertaken under the NREGS. To m aintain the transparency, I would 
suggest for consideration of the hon. Minister that technical estimates to be displayed at all 
worksides in simple local language. A progress repor t has to be given by an independent 
authority to local vigilance committee. Then all th e public works sanctioned or undertaken 
should be in the public domain with physical, techn ical and financial details through notice 
boards, websites, etc. 
Then the idea of this entire programme is to create physical assets. But, there is a problem 
in this. What the people are doing is that they are  taking up the work and completing and 
again they are showing in the registers the same wo rk by manipulation and getting money 
from the Government. Or, sometimes, there will be duplication. So, to remove this problem, I 
suggest for consideration of the hon. Minister to m aintain an asset register with a unique 
number to each work to prevent duplication. At the same time, there should also be maps of

the physical assets so created so that there would not be any duplication a;id we can also avoid 
sanctioning money for the same work. 
The other problem in the NREGS is that, there is a cash component and Foodgrain component. 
There is a problem that many people are demanding f or giving cash instead of cash and 
foodgrains. There is a problem in providing foodgrains as they sometime do not reach in time and, 
as we all know, the quality offoodgrains is also very bad. So, I suggest that entire wage payment be 
made in cash and do not couple it with foodgrains. This will solve a major problem of delay and 
inadequate remuneration.Finally; we also know that the States are deviating funds given by GOI 
under NREGS. I suggest for consideration of the hon. Minister that wherever it is found that the 
States have diverted funds either through vigilance reports or otherwise, those States should be 
penalised in their grants and the States which are implementing the programme well should be 
rewarded by giving more funds.
